w: William Rufus raised this castle around 1092 inside an old Roman fort to guard a Pennine pass - the Scots burned it in 1174, and after a 1521 Christmas feast ended in disaster, it took Lady Anne Clifford until 1661 to put it right. A second fire in 1666 finished it for good; it's been slowly collapsing since 1800.
s: Castle rebuilt by Lady Anne Clifford, twice burned
_facts: Ruined castle in Brough, Cumbria, built by William Rufus c.1092 within the Roman fort of Verterae
Destroyed by the Scots in 1174; rebuilt; fire after a 1521 Christmas feast destroyed it again
Restored by Lady Anne Clifford 1659-1661; another fire in 1666; given to the state in 1921, now run by English Heritage

w: Built in 1090 by Norman baron Robert de Romille at the head of Skipton's High Street, this is one of the best-preserved medieval castles in England - Grade I listed, still standing where it's stood for nearly a thousand years, and now split between a private residence and a steady stream of visitors.
s: Norman castle still standing atop the High Street
_facts: Well-preserved Grade I listed medieval castle in Skipton, North Yorkshire
Built in 1090 by Robert de Romille, a Norman baron
Now a tourist attraction and private residence, at the north end of Skipton's High Street

w: The lowest of the Yorkshire Three Peaks at 694 metres, Pen-y-ghent hides a cave system beneath its slopes - Hunt Pot, Hull Pot, and water that resurfaces miles away at Brants Gill. In 2004 a body found near Sell Gill Hole, dubbed the "Lady of the Hills" by the press, added a darker footnote to the fell's story.
s: Three Peaks fell with caves and an unsolved mystery
_facts: Fell in the Yorkshire Dales, lowest of the Three Peaks at 694m, 1.9 miles east of Horton in Ribblesdale
Geological features include Hunt Pot and Hull Pot, feeding an extensive cave system rising at Brants Gill head
In 2004 a body dubbed by media the 'Lady of the Hills' was found near the entrance to Sell Gill Hole

w: A lonely ruin above a bend in the River Eden in Mallerstang Dale, overlooked by Wild Boar Fell and Mallerstang Edge - its name carries an echo of Arthurian legend, though the stonework is honestly medieval rather than mythic. Grade I listed, near the hamlet of Outhgill, it's one of the quietest ruins in the Dales.
s: Lonely ruin with an Arthurian name in Mallerstang Dale
_facts: Ruin in Mallerstang Dale, Cumbria, south of Kirkby Stephen, near the hamlet of Outhgill
Stands above a bend in the River Eden, overlooked by Wild Boar Fell and Mallerstang Edge
Grade I listed building

w: A French chateau transplanted onto a County Durham hillside, built to house the art hoard of John Bowes and his wife Josephine - El Greco, Goya and Canaletto among the paintings, plus porcelain and tapestries. Its real showstopper is the Silver Swan, a life-size automaton that preens and appears to catch a fish.
s: A French chateau housing a fish-catching silver swan
_facts: Art gallery in Barnard Castle, County Durham, designed by Jules Pellechet and John Edward Watson, opened 1892
Built to house the art collection of John Bowes and wife Josephine Benoite Coffin-Chevallier
Holds paintings by El Greco, Goya, Canaletto, Fragonard and Boucher; showpiece is the Silver Swan automaton

w: The second-highest peak in the Yorkshire Dales at 723 metres, and one of the Three Peaks alongside Whernside and Pen-y-ghent, it draws walkers doing the circuit as much as naturalists. A large stretch of its slopes is a protected Site of Special Scientific Interest, now home to the Wild Ingleborough rewilding project.
s: Three Peaks summit and rewilding project site
_facts: Second-highest mountain in the Yorkshire Dales at 723m, one of the Yorkshire Three Peaks
Frequently climbed as part of the Three Peaks walk
Large part designated Site of Special Scientific Interest and National Nature Reserve, home to the Wild Ingleborough project

w: One of only eight upland alkaline lakes in Europe, sitting at 377 metres - the highest marl lake in Britain - this glacial pool inspired Charles Kingsley to set his 1863 fable The Water-Babies here. The National Trust owns it now; the field centre that once studied its rare ecology closed for good in 2022.
s: Glacial lake that inspired The Water-Babies
_facts: Glacial lake near Malham in the Yorkshire Dales, one of only eight upland alkaline lakes in Europe
At 377m altitude, the highest marl lake in the UK
Inspired Charles Kingsley's 1863 novel The Water-Babies; owned by the National Trust, its Field Studies Council centre closed in 2022

w: A 12th-century Augustinian priory dissolved by Henry VIII in 1539, its gatehouse converted into a country house for the Duke of Devonshire while the ruined nave carries on as a working church, Bolton Priory. Miles of estate walking trails and a steam railway terminus make the ruins as much a destination as a relic.
s: Dissolved priory that's still a working parish church
_facts: 12th-century Augustinian priory in Wharfedale, North Yorkshire, closed in the 1539 Dissolution of the Monasteries
Gatehouse extended into Bolton Abbey Hall, owned by the Duke of Devonshire; medieval church remains in use as Bolton Priory parish church
Estate open to visitors with many miles of walking routes; Embsay & Bolton Abbey Steam Railway terminates 1.5 miles away

w: Henry II raised this stone keep between 1170 and 1174 inside the walls of the old Roman fort of Lavatrae, right on the road that's now the A66. It held off the Scots in the Great Revolt of 1173-74 but was looted by rebels in 1322 and later stripped for its stone - English Heritage lets you in free, daylight hours only.
s: Free-to-visit keep built inside a Roman fort's walls
_facts: Medieval castle in Bowes, County Durham, built within the perimeter of the Roman fort of Lavatrae on the A66
Stone structure replaced an earlier timber castle 1170-1174 on orders of Henry II; withstood Scottish attack in 1173-74 but looted by rebels in 1322
Largely dismantled after the English Civil War; now owned by English Heritage, free admission during daylight hours

w: Nine tall cairns, some once over four metres high, crown this Pennine summit for reasons nobody has nailed down - a boundary marker between old Westmorland and Swaledale is the best guess. They sit on the Coast to Coast Walk near a watershed between rivers running to opposite coasts, and beat the trig point for views.
s: Nine mysterious cairns of uncertain purpose
_facts: Summit of Hartley Fell in the Pennines, near Kirkby Stephen, within the North Pennines AONB
Named for the Nine Standards, a group of cairns near the summit, some originally over four metres high, of uncertain original purpose - possibly a boundary marker between Westmorland and Swaledale
On the Coast to Coast Walk between Kirkby Stephen and Keld; offers a better viewpoint than the actual trig point

w: Fell Beck disappears into this pothole and drops 98 metres in one go - the highest unbroken waterfall in Britain, into one of the largest underground chambers open to the surface. It was Britain's deepest known shaft until a Derbyshire cave overtook it in 1999; the water resurfaces nearby at Ingleborough Cave.
s: Britain's highest freefall waterfall drops underground
_facts: Natural cave/pothole on the southern slopes of Ingleborough, 98 metres deep with Fell Beck flowing in
Held record as deepest known shaft in Britain until Titan in Derbyshire was found in 1999
Retains records for highest freefall waterfall in the UK and largest underground chamber naturally open to the surface; resurfaces at Ingleborough Cave

w: A show cave near Clapham where the waters of Gaping Gill resurface after their underground plunge, its public stretch running 500 metres through a fossil gallery hung with stalagmite formations. Divers have since traced the flooded passages beyond it onward to Lake Pluto and a submerged network few will ever see.
s: Show cave where Gaping Gill's waters resurface
_facts: Show cave near Clapham, North Yorkshire, formerly known as Clapham Caves
Public section follows a fossil gallery for about 500 metres, well decorated with stalagmite formations
Beyond the show cave, divers have connected passages to Gaping Gill and Lake Pluto

w: Third-highest fell in the Dales and the high point of Wensleydale, with the Pennine Way crossing its 716-metre summit - decades of boot traffic wore a 70-metre scar into the moor before flagstones were laid in 1996 to save it. Its slopes are also Britain's most southerly outpost for the rare yellow marsh saxifrage.
s: Pennine Way summit saved by a flagstone path
_facts: Third-highest mountain in the Yorkshire Dales at 716m, highest point in Wensleydale
Pennine Way crosses its summit; erosion from foot traffic alleviated since 1996 by a flagstone path
Most southerly remaining outpost in Britain for the yellow marsh saxifrage

w: A Premonstratensian abbey above the River Tees near Barnard Castle, dissolved along with the rest and left to decay into the scheduled ruin standing today. English Heritage keeps it free to visit - a quieter, less-touristed counterpart to the bigger Yorkshire abbeys, historically counted part of the North Riding.
s: Free-to-visit ruined abbey above the River Tees
_facts: Ruined Premonstratensian abbey in County Durham, 1.5 miles southeast of Barnard Castle on the River Tees
Historically within the North Riding of Yorkshire
Protected as a Scheduled Ancient Monument, maintained by English Heritage, free admission

w: Britain's longest cave system, some 41 miles of passage between Leck Fell and Casterton Fell - first broken into in 1946 when two cavers found a gap that opened onto a 34-metre shaft. Decades of exploring and diving have since stitched Lancaster Hole, Pippikin Pot and Lost Johns' Cave into one vast, still-growing map.
s: Britain's longest cave system - 41 miles and counting
_facts: Longest and most complex cave system in Britain as of 2011, around 41 miles of passages spanning Leck and Casterton Fells
First entrance, Lancaster Hole, found in 1946 opening onto a 110-foot shaft
Connected over decades to Link Pot and Pippikin Pot (1978), and to Lost Johns' Cave by diving in 1989

w: This viaduct carries the Settle-Carlisle line across Batty Moss, built from 1869 by a workforce of up to 2,300 men in shanty towns at its base - over a hundred died before the last stone went in, in 1874. British Rail tried to close the line in the 1980s; public outcry saved it, and trains cross it still.
s: Viaduct that cost 100+ lives, then survived closure
_facts: Grade II* listed viaduct carrying the Settle-Carlisle railway across Batty Moss at Ribblehead
Built from 1869 by up to 2,300 men living in shanty towns; over 100 died during construction; completed by end of 1874
British Rail proposed closure in the 1980s; public lobbying saved the line in 1989

w: A motte-and-bailey stronghold whose earthwork mound still rises over the village, garrisoned in 1129-30 by a single knight, ten sergeants, a gatekeeper and a watchman - a skeleton crew for a real castle. Confiscated from the rebellious Mowbray family in 1322, only the mound survives to mark where it stood.
s: Castle mound once garrisoned by just a dozen men
_facts: Motte castle with two baileys in Burton in Lonsdale, North Yorkshire
Pipe Rolls record its 1129-1130 garrison as a knight, ten sergeants, a gatekeeper and a watchman
Confiscated from the Mowbrays in 1322 for opposing Edward II; the mound is still visible

w: A sprawling grass moorland above Kendal, less dramatic than its Lakeland neighbours but with its own small feud: the landowner has long fought to keep walkers off the final stretch, though a right of way crosses most of the fell. Views take in the Howgills, the Lakes and the Dales - if you can reach the top.
s: Moorland fell with a landowner's summit stand-off
_facts: Highest point of the high ground between Kendal and the M6, a grassy moorland fell in Cumbria
Provides views of the Howgill Fells, the Lake District and the Yorkshire Dales
Landowner strongly opposed to use of the summit track; right of way instead follows a boggy route that stops short of the top

w: Straddling the Lancashire-Yorkshire border, its 627-metre summit is the second-highest point in modern Lancashire, just inside Yorkshire Dales National Park. The Three Men of Gragareth - tall cairns above Leck Fell House - watch a hillside riddled with caves, and one of Britain's highest dry stone walls runs the ridge.
s: Border fell with tall cairns and a record-high wall
_facts: Mountain straddling Lancashire/North Yorkshire border, 627m, second-highest point in modern Lancashire
Summit lies within the 2016 Yorkshire Dales National Park boundary; contains caves including Lost John's Cave, Rumbling Hole and Ireby Fell Cavern
Three Men of Gragareth cairns above Leck Fell House; ridge wall said to be one of the highest dry stone walls in the country

w: Highest point in the Howgill Fells at 676 metres, usually climbed from Sedbergh on what Alfred Wainwright called the classic high-level walk on these hills. A weathered standing stone leans 400 yards northeast of the trig point, and on a clear day the flat summit opens onto a 20-mile skyline of the Lake District.
s: Howgills summit and Wainwright's classic high walk
_facts: Highest point in the Howgill Fells at 676m, in Cumbria near the Yorkshire Dales
Wainwright described the Sedbergh ascent to Calders and The Calf as 'the classic high-level walk on the Howgill Fells'
A 'reclining' standing stone lies 400 yards northeast of the summit trig point; views extend to a 20-mile Lakeland skyline
